newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Fight over media control intensifies in Russia.
newsitem.headline: Fight over media control intensifies in Russia.

text.p: A decision by Russian parliament to set strict limits on television coverage of its sessions intensified a fierce debate on Thursday over media freedoms and the politicial influence of a new generation of press barons.

The opposition-dominated State Duma lower house voted on Wednesday to give its press service the sole right to film debates, barring independent filming and prompting the Kremlin into cries of censorship.

The decision followed months of complaints by opposition deputies that newspapers and television have become political weapons in the hands of the state, a few rich entepreneurs and major companies which are their shareholders.
One result is that the liberal Izvestia daily is under fire for making relentless attacks on Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and the government says some ministers are victims of a hate campaign.
Behind it all is a debate on media freedoms more than five years after the Soviet Union and communist rule collapsed.
"Open political interests and contradictions are behind the normal market processes of buying and redestributing shares," the liberal Moscow News weekly said in its latest edition.
Independent media were the first symbol of post-Soviet Russia and were instrumental in the first democratic transformations.
But politicians and financial bosses quickly grasped the media's ability to influence public opinion and their profitability.
Media empires are now emerging, powerful financial groups are launching their own publications and others are trying to consolidate their stakes in ones that are well established.
Some experts say the fight for the media market goes beyond financial interests and reflects a major role in politics.

"In all probability, a large-scale plan is being implemented by those people who have realised all too well the role of the mass media, which managed to raise the rating of one of the candidates in the presidential campaign to victory from only six percent," Moscow News said.
It was a reference to last year's presidential election in which Yeltsin was heavily backed by the media.
Yeltsin said earlier this month that the independence of the media was one of the biggest gains of democratic Russia and that he would protect it.
A government spokesmen took up the same theme this week, but at the same time criticised a host of publications for stories which he said were incorrect.
"We are witnessing a continued campaign, which may or may not be orchestrated, aimed at discrediting some leaders of the government," government spokesman Igor Shabdurasulov said.
Sergei Markov, a political analyst at the Moscow office of the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, said the days of full press freedoms and independence had long gone.
"The mass media are far from being independent," he said. "Certain political and financial groups control and use them for their own purposes."

He cited Wednesday's decision in the Duma. Until now television companies had been allowed to film debates but the deputies were unhappy over pictures of sleeping deputies, multiple-voting or replays of awkward or dubious quotes.
The new rules allow television companies, both Russian and foreign, to use the official footage but each of them has to work out conditions under which it will receive the material.

Markov called the decision "a major mistake by parliament". But he acknowledged that the coverage by the main Russian television channels -- some with the state or people who are direct or indirect opponents of the legislature as shareholders -- created a negative image of the Duma.
Tensions are also high over many popular newspapers.
Izvestia started a row by reprinting an article from a French newspaper over the extent of Chernomyrdin's personal wealth, which the prime minister shrugged off.

Izvestia has accused the government of hitting back by using its state influence over a major oil company with 41 percent of the newspaper's shares. The daily says the oil company criticised Izvestia's decision to reprint the article.
"The mass media are being used like simple goods such as oil or gas and this is being used not just to achieve the commercial aims of big business," Izvestia said on Thursday.
"This is being used to restore political censorship in the Communist Party style because big business itself depends on the government to a huge extent."
